title: Inline Skating in Cold Weather: Why Your Skates Feel Different on a Winter Morning
thumbnail_text: Why your skates feel slower on cold mornings

scenes.heading: Inline Skating in Cold Weather
scenes.sub: Why your skates feel different on a winter morning, and what to change
scenes.narration: Your skates feel slower and looser on a cold morning, and there is a simple reason for it. In the next few minutes you will learn what cold does to your wheels, your bearings and your body, and exactly what to change. Three things happen at once. Cold urethane stiffens and grips less. Cold bearing oil thickens and drags for the first few minutes. And a cold road often carries a thin film of dew that you cannot see until a wheel slides on it. None of that is a fault in your skates. It is physics, and you can manage it.

scenes.heading: Same wheel, two temperatures
scenes.chapter: What cold does to a wheel
scenes.narration: Start with the wheels. Urethane is sensitive to temperature. Warm it, and it softens, flexes more under load and grips harder. On the left, the warm wheel squashes into a wider contact patch, so it holds the road well. Cool it, and the compound stiffens. On the right, the cold wheel flexes less, its contact patch shrinks, and it holds the surface with less bite. So a cold wheel behaves like a harder wheel than the grade printed on the box. That is why skaters wash out on the first corner of a winter session. Your technique did not go backwards overnight. The wheel is simply harder than the one you set your lean for yesterday afternoon.

scenes.heading: Your first laps are the riskiest
scenes.chapter: Why the first laps are risky
bullets: Wheels warm up from load and the road
At dawn, none of that heat exists yet
Your muscles are cold and slow too
Most early crashes happen here
scenes.narration: Timing matters a lot on a cold morning. A wheel reaches its working temperature partly from the road surface and partly from the heat it makes as it flexes and recovers under load. At six in the morning, none of that heat exists yet. So your first laps are the least grippy laps of the whole session. They are also the laps when your muscles are coldest and your reactions are slowest. Put those two things together, and you have the moment when most early morning crashes happen. Treat those first laps as information, not as a time trial.

scenes.heading: The first fifteen minutes
scenes.narration: Bearing oil also changes with temperature. Cold oil is thicker, and thicker oil takes more energy as the balls roll through it. This timeline shows what happens. At minute zero, the oil is thick, the roll is short and the wheels are hard. As you skate, the oil warms and thins, and grip comes back. By around minute fifteen, roll and grip are back to normal. So do not judge a set of bearings on a cold morning. If you want to check whether a bearing is worn, do it indoors at room temperature, and listen for grit and roughness rather than timing the spin. And if your bearings still feel slow after the first ten minutes, that is not the cold. That is grit, water or wear.

scenes.heading: Do not flood your bearings
bullets: One drop of skate oil per bearing
Extra oil collects dust and drags
Heavy household oil adds drag
Slow after ten minutes means clean them
scenes.narration: Do not try to fix cold drag by flooding the bearing with oil. Heavy oils protect but drag. Very thin oils feel fast for ten minutes and then leave the bearing dry. A purpose made skate bearing oil sits between those two extremes. One drop per bearing is the whole dose, all year round. More than that collects dust and adds drag of its own. If your bearings really are slow once everything is warm, the fix is to clean them, dry them fully and put one fresh drop in each. The routine is the same for steel and ceramic bearings.

scenes.heading: Dew, fog and the film you cannot see
bullets: Painted lines, tiles and metal covers stay damp
Shade under flyovers and trees stays wet
Scout your first lap slowly
Thick fog means train indoors
scenes.narration: In most of India, the bigger cold weather hazard is not the temperature. It is the moisture. On a clear winter night, the road loses heat and water condenses on it. By first light, smooth tarmac can carry an invisible film of dew that behaves like light rain. Painted lines, tiled sections, metal covers and polished concrete are the worst. They stay damp long after the rest of the road looks dry. Shade is the trap. A road that is dry in the sun can be wet under a flyover, beside a wall or under trees. So scout your first lap slowly and note where the shade sits. And if the fog is so thick that you cannot see a vehicle at a comfortable stopping distance, take the session to a closed track or the gym.

scenes.heading: Skate your grippier wheels
bullets: Choose grip over roll when it is cold
XFirm over XXFirm if you own both
A Firm set helps on slick surfaces
Round wheels grip better than worn ones
scenes.narration: When grip is scarce, skate the grippiest compound you own, not the fastest rolling one. Race wheels come in named firmness grades. For most skaters, the winter choice is between an XFirm set and an XXFirm set. XFirm is the grippier of the two. XXFirm is harder and tuned for roll and straight line speed. If you own both, skate the XFirm. If you have a softer Firm set from the wet season, that is the one to reach for. Do not raid your old, worn training set hoping for more grip. Worn, coned wheels give you less contact, not more. And be honest about the limit. A grippier wheel does not make a dewy underpass safe. On those mornings, the answer is a slower first lap and a shorter session.

scenes.heading: Cold morning session order
scenes.narration: Your body is stiffer in the cold too. The push in inline speed skating loads the groin, hip flexors and lower back through a long, deep range. A stiff body asked for full power in the first five minutes is how strains happen. So keep the same warm up, but roughly double it. Stage one is off the skates: easy movement, mobility and activation, for twelve to twenty minutes. Stage two is ten minutes of easy rolling with short strokes and no lean. Stage three builds a deeper position and tests your grip. Only then comes stage four, the hard efforts. Cold aches that ease once you are warm are normal. But sharp pain, swelling, numbness, a joint that gives way, or pain that lasts more than a few days is worth seeing a physiotherapist or doctor about.

scenes.heading: What to wear on a cold morning
bullets: A skinsuit is built for air, not warmth
Warm up in a layer over your suit
Strip down close to the main effort
Cover your hands and ears
scenes.narration: A race suit is built for air, not for warmth. A close, aerodynamic cut is exactly what you want at race pace. It is not what you want on a cold start line for twenty minutes. So warm up in a tracksuit or a thermal layer over your suit, and strip down shortly before the effort that matters. Cover your hands and your ears, because your fingers lose dexterity quickly in the cold, and you want a full grip if you have to put a hand down. After the session, do not leave a damp suit in a bag. Wash it gently and dry it away from direct heat.

scenes.heading: Condensation is the real rust risk
bullets: Cold metal collects water indoors
Wipe wheels and bearings down
Air dry, never in a zipped bag
Spin each wheel and listen
scenes.narration: Here is the part that catches people out. Cold metal brought into a warm, humid room collects condensation, just like a cold glass of water. That moisture lands on your bearing shields, axles and frame. If your skates go straight into a zipped bag, it sits there for hours. So treat a cold morning like a wet one. Wipe the wheels and the outside of the bearings, loosen the boots, and leave the skates where air can move around them. A shaded balcony or a shelf under a ceiling fan works well. Once everything is at room temperature, spin each wheel by hand and listen. A short or gritty roll means it is time to clean, dry and oil.

scenes.heading: Your cold morning checklist
bullets: Check the forecast for fog
Scout shade, paint, tiles and covers
Skate your grippiest, roundest set
Double the warm up, start off skates
Wipe down and air dry afterwards
scenes.narration: Here is your checklist. Check the forecast for fog, not just the temperature, because visibility decides whether a road session happens at all. Scout the first lap slowly, and note where the shade, paint, tiles and metal covers sit. Skate the grippiest compound you own, and keep your newest, roundest set for cold, damp days. Double your usual warm up, start it off the skates, and give the first ten minutes on wheels to easy rolling. Warm up in a layer over your suit. And afterwards, wipe down and air dry your skates, because condensation does the rusting.

scenes.heading: Treat the first laps as information, not a time trial
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: If you remember one thing, make it this. On a cold morning, your wheels, your oil and your body all start the session cold. Give all three time to warm up, and save your hardest efforts for the second half. The full guide, with the wheel grades and the whole cold weather routine, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
